description: I'm Tiago, Information Systems undergrad at IF Goiano with skills in Web Dev, 3D/WebXR, and Figma. We're tackling "The Earth Information Jukebox" to turn NASA Earth imagery into real-time music and accessible soundscapes. Join us! We have a clear MVP plan ready to build. Looking for teammates interested in Frontend/UI, Audio/Music, NASA Data/Storytelling, or Pitch/Video.
summary: Ecos da Terra turns NASA Earth visualizations into sound, so anyone can explore our planet by ear, including the 2.2 billion people living with vision impairment. A scanning bar sweeps official NASA Scientific Visualization Studio maps: aerosols, night lights, lightning seen from the ISS and GEDI forest height. Each phenomenon becomes its own instrument: Saharan dust, wildfire smoke and city lights each sound different. Higher on the map means a higher pitch, and more data means louder sound, following NASA’s own sonification method. An automatic voice describes the image, the sound rules and every point the user explores, saying what it is and where on Earth. Users can explore with a mouse, touch, the keyboard, or just their eyes: on-device AI tracks the iris after a voice-guided calibration that needs no sight. Everything runs in one HTML file in any browser, with no login and no server, and images never leave the device. Ecos da Terra brings Earth science to classrooms, museums and homes, so blind and sighted people can hear our planet change, together.
details:
What it does and how it works. Ecos da Terra is an “Earth Information Jukebox.” The user picks one of four NASA SVS visualizations, or uploads their own photo or video, and first hears a sound legend: each color says its name and plays its sound. Pressing play starts a sweep across the map. An HTML5 Canvas pixel reader counts the colors in each column. Scientific rules for each map, based on NASA’s own legends, translate color into phenomenon and phenomenon into sound. The Web Audio API synthesizes stereo, pentatonic sound live: horizontal position sets stereo panning, latitude sets pitch, and the amount of data sets volume. Users can stop at any point to hear a spoken description of the phenomenon and its region, such as “Saharan dust, over North Africa.” For uploaded images, on-device AI (Human/TensorFlow.js) recognizes NASA-style maps or everyday objects.

Eye control. For users with limited motor control, the front camera and MediaPipe face and iris models (478 landmarks) estimate gaze entirely on the device. A voice-guided calibration tells the user to keep their head straight and look center, left, right, up and down, with directional tones. Afterwards, holding the gaze on a point describes it, the corners change maps or play and pause, and a long blink also plays or pauses. Audio description turns on automatically.

Benefits and impact. It makes NASA open data accessible to blind and low-vision people, and gives sighted learners a second way to understand complex data. One file works offline, so it fits schools with poor connectivity.

Tools.

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no framework and no backend.

Web Audio API, Web Speech API and the Piper neural voice (ONNX Runtime Web).

Human/TensorFlow.js with MediaPipe models.

NASA SVS Earth Information Center data (#5669, #5313, #5011, #4950) and the sonification method in SVS #13786.

It runs on any laptop or phone; eye control needs WebGL.

Creativity and design choices.

Every sound is tied to a real NASA legend, not decoration.

It is designed for privacy (nothing is uploaded) and works in Portuguese and English.

It offers full keyboard use, screen-reader announcements and three text sizes.

Next step: testing with blind and low-vision users, as the deck says: “made with them, not just for them.”
